title: Pointer lifetime, dangling pointers and object validity (CodeSaathi extension)
learningObjectives: Explain object lifetime and how it constrains pointer validity.
Identify dangling pointers caused by returning addresses of local automatic objects.
Release dynamically allocated storage exactly once when ownership ends.
Avoid using pointers after free and avoid double-free errors.
Use clear ownership contracts and set released pointer variables to NULL when appropriate.

understand.concept: An object's lifetime is the period during which the object exists according to the C language rules. A pointer becomes dangling when the object it designated no longer exists or its allocated storage has been released. Dereferencing a dangling pointer has undefined behavior. Correct C programs make ownership, lifetime and release responsibilities explicit.
understand.whyItMatters: A pointer can be non-null and still be invalid. Lifetime mistakes cause use-after-scope, use-after-free and subtle memory corruption.
understand.analogy: Treat a function or pointer operation as an explicit contract between caller and callee.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal rules for types, object lifetime, scope and linkage.

explain.narrative:
## 1. Object lifetime

An automatic local object generally exists only while execution is within its block. A pointer to that object must not be used after the block ends. Returning the address of a local automatic variable creates a dangling pointer.

## 2. Dynamic storage duration

Memory allocated by malloc, calloc or realloc remains allocated until it is released with free or the allocation is otherwise replaced. The program must track who owns the allocation and which code is responsible for releasing it.

## 3. Use after free

After free releases an allocation, pointers to that storage must not be dereferenced. Freeing the same allocation more than once is also undefined behavior. Setting the owning pointer to NULL after free can prevent accidental reuse through that variable, but other aliases may still dangle.

## 4. Ownership contracts

Document whether a function borrows a pointer, takes ownership, or returns a newly allocated object. A borrowed pointer must not outlive its target. The owner must release allocated storage exactly once.

## 5. Handle failure paths

Check allocation results before dereferencing. Ensure every failure path releases allocations already acquired. Keep cleanup logic structured so early returns do not leak resources or access released objects.

examples.title: Return dynamically allocated storage with clear ownership
examples.explanation: The function returns allocated storage, not the address of a local automatic object. The caller owns the allocation and releases it.

examples.title: Do not return a local address
examples.explanation: The pointer is borrowed only during the lifetime of local. The example does not retain or return the address beyond that lifetime.

practise.guidedTask: Write a C program demonstrating CL5.9. State the relevant input, pointer or conversion contract, then compile and trace the normal and failure paths.
practise.independentTask: Create a second example for CL5.9 that exercises a boundary or invalid state. Add checks, document the ownership or input rules, and explain why unsafe behavior is avoided.

questions.prompt: When does a pointer to a local automatic variable become dangling?
options: After the local object's lifetime ends
Immediately when its address is taken
questions.answer: After the local object's lifetime ends
questions.explanation: The pointer cannot be used after the designated object ceases to exist.

questions.prompt: What should happen to dynamically allocated storage when its owner is finished?
options: Release it exactly once with free
questions.answer: Release it exactly once with free
questions.explanation: The owner is responsible for releasing allocated storage.

options: Accessing an object through a pointer after its allocation has been released
questions.answer: Accessing an object through a pointer after its allocation has been released
questions.explanation: The storage no longer contains a live allocated object.

questions.prompt: Does setting one pointer to NULL invalidate every alias to the same allocation?
options: No; other pointer copies may still dangle
Yes, all aliases are automatically updated
Only if the pointer is global
questions.answer: No; other pointer copies may still dangle
questions.explanation: Assigning NULL changes only that pointer object.

questions.prompt: What should an ownership contract describe?
options: Who may use the object and who must release allocated storage
questions.answer: Who may use the object and who must release allocated storage
questions.explanation: Clear ownership prevents leaks, double frees and dangling references.
